senses: A civilian dress when worn by a member of the military or the police, or casual dress when worn by a pupil of a school who normally would wear uniform.
ety: Borrowed from Ottoman Turkish مفتی (müfti), from Arabic مُفْتِي (muftī, “fatwa-deliverer”, literally “deliverer of formal opinion”).
examples: He had a suit of summer mufti, and a broad-brimmed blue beaver hat looped with leaves broken from the hedgerows in the lanes, and a Leander scarf tucked full of flowers: loosestrife, meadowrue, orchis, ragged-robin.
The innate reluctance of the Englishman to make himself conspicuous has stood him here in good stead. Except on special occasions, the British officers are almost always in mufti.
The sailors in mufti returned with 140 quarts of Bar's Leak, half of which was poured into the condenser.

senses: Poured out freely; profuse.
Disposed to pour out freely; prodigal.
ety: Borrowed from Middle French effuser, from Latin effusus, past participle of effundere (“to pour out”).
examples: So should our joy be very effuse.
No wanton waste amid effuse expence

senses: Someone or thing who lives in a place.
A possible value for a type.
ety: From Middle English inhabitantes (n. plural) and inhabitaunt (adj.), from Old French inhabitant, from Latin inhabitāns, present participle of inhabitō (“to inhabit”), from in- (“in”) + habitō (“to dwell”) (frequentative of habeō (“to hold”), from Proto-Indo-European *ghabh- (“to seize, take, hold, have”). By surface analysis, inhabit + -ant.
examples: I believed it in the same way one of you might believe there are inhabitants in the planet Mars. I knew once a Scotch sailmaker who was certain, dead sure, there were people in Mars.

It was obvious to the inhabitants of the small coastal town of Bridport that in the midst of these squabbles their need for a railway was going to be overlooked, and they decided to take the matter into their own hands.
One way to observe this connection with mathematics is by mapping each type to its cardinality, a count of the inhabitants of that type.

senses: To urge a person; to press on; to incite to action or motion via intrinsic motivation.
To drive forward; to propel an object, to provide an impetus for motion or action.
ety: From Middle English impellen, borrowed from Latin impellō.
examples: I feel impelled to reply to Roger Henry's letter about my article on being denied an apartment. I truly resent any insinuation that I "slunk back into that rotting old closet."
The wind impelled the kayaks toward the shore.

senses: Somewhat shrill.
ety: From shrill + -y.
examples: The night—its silence—its rest, was rent in twain by a savage, a sharp, a shrilly sound that ran from end to end of Thornfield Hall.

senses: A traditional Chinese dumpling of glutinous rice stuffed with a savoury or sweet filling, wrapped in large flat leaves, and cooked by steaming or boiling.
ety: Borrowed from the Hanyu Pinyin romanization of Mandarin 粽子 (zòngzi), from 粽 (zòng, “dumpling of glutinous rice wrapped in leaves”) + 子 (zi, diminutive suffix).
examples: A week or two before the festival, villagers would prepare glutinous rice wrapped in bamboo leaves before cooking, commonly known as zongzi or chang (in Hokkien).
Sunny ordered four zongzis or dumplings and, out of tradition, haggled with the woman until they agreed on a price.

senses: A prophylactic condom.
Any device or mechanism intended to prevent harmful consequences.
ety: From Latin prophylacticus, from Ancient Greek προφυλακτικός (prophulaktikós, “prophylactic”).
examples: It is not clear whether such education is to be directed to homosexuals (for whom prophylactics are not a contraceptive) or to heterosexuals as well (for whom prophylactics are a contraceptive).
Some men put the prophylactic on just the tip of the penis: this is a mistake, because the prophylactic will come off.
The securities laws are a prophylactic against stock fraud.

senses: A red powder, made from saffron or turmeric, used ceremonially by Hindu women to make various markings on the body, especially the tilak.
ety: From Hindi कुमकुम (kumkum) from Sanskrit कुङ्कुम (kuṅkuma).
examples: A maid passed her the gold thali with a lamp and kumkum and turmeric powder in it.
Saubhagya Devi sent Alak Kishori to fetch kumkum.

senses: The lower metallic cap at the end of a sword's scabbard.
The tip of a fox's tail.
ety: From Middle English chape, from Old French chape (“a churchman's cope, a cover, a chape”), from Latin cappa, itself derived from Latin caput (“the head”). Doublet of cap, cape, and cope.
examples: The scabbard ended in a chape, which took two forms: sometimes it terminated in a ball, and sometimes in a crescent or fish-tail.

senses: Any agent, natural or artificial, that acts to preserve, especially when added to food.
ety: From Old French preservatif, from Medieval Latin praeservativus.
examples: Salt, sugar, and acid all act as preservatives when making pickles.

senses: Having a flavor or essence of mint.
ety: From mint + -y.
examples: Moroccan curried crab and streaks of minty, lemony yogurt add luxury to a supersimple zucchini soup ($14).

senses: A little mass of lead, or the like, attached to a line, and used by builders, etc., to indicate a vertical direction.
The perpendicular direction or position.
ety: From Middle English plumbe, plumme, from Old French *plombe, from Latin plumba, plural of plumbum.
examples: Customers turned away from rickety chairs, stands of drawers that refused to open, or had no handles, lop-sided wardrobes whose doors were out of plumb or whose mirrors were cracked.

senses: A pasta of North African origin made of crushed and steamed semolina.
ety: Borrowed from French couscous, from Arabic كُسْكُس (kuskus), from a Berber language. First use appears c. 1593.
examples: Karou took the plate of couscous and vegetables.

senses: An ornamented or painted ball or boss fastened at each end of the stick on which manuscripts were rolled.
ety: Borrowed from Latin umbilīcus (“navel”).
examples: The ends of the umbilicus were called cornua (i.e. horns) in Latin, and were usually adorned with some pretty device

senses: An employee, a worker; now especially a Japanese white-collar worker who works long hours yet has an insignificant position within the corporate hierarchy.
ety: Phono-semantic matching of Japanese サラリーマン (sararīman), itself a wasei eigo (和製英語; pseudo-anglicism) derived from salary + man.
examples: In this way, the salaryman was both a progressive social stratum and an intellectual class.

senses: The quality of being trivial or unimportant.
Something which is trivial or unimportant.
ety: From trivial + -ity.
examples: I propose to devote the remainder of mine to it, and can only regret the wasted years that lie behind me, squandered in trivialities.
Yes, I have a case. After a month of trivialities and stagnation the wheels move once more.

senses: Grim or severe in manner or appearance.
Lacking decoration; trivial; not extravagant or gaudy.
Adhering to the economic policy of austerity.
Harsh; astringent.
ety: From Ancient Greek αὐστηρός (austērós, “bitter, harsh, astringent”), having the specific meaning “making the tongue dry” (originally used of fruits, wines), related to αὔω (aúō, “to singe”), αὖος (aûos, “dry”).
examples: The headmistress was an austere old woman.
The interior of the church was as austere as the parishioners were dour.
So we come, at above street level, into the city, and to Canterbury East Station (9.8 miles). It is an austere, rather barn-like structure, with a high roof over the two platforms.

senses: To make (something) into a liquid.
To distort and warp (an image).
To become liquid.
ety: From Middle English liquefien, from Anglo-Norman liquefier, from Latin liquefacere.
examples: We’ll liquefy this rock by heating it in a furnace until it melts and flows out.
Place crayfish and fresh pepper in a blender, add small water, liquefy and cook for 20 minutes or until tender.
The substance liquefied upon heating.

senses: An android (humanoid robot) in female form.
ety: From gyno- + android.
examples: She was obviously a skillful surgeon. She expertly cleaned and sterilized the gaping holes in the gynoid’s chest and back.
She is embodied as a bright blue feminized robot, much like the mechanized gynoids in the classic film Metropolis (1928).

senses: To subject to a penalty, especially for the infringement of a rule or regulation.
ety: From penal + -ize.
examples: Women should not be penalized or forced out of the workplace simply because they become pregnant. UPS, in fact, has come around to that position. It now offers light-duty accommodations to pregnant women who need them.

senses: The transition between poses executed in succession, often timed with regular breathing.
A style of yoga based on a flow between sequential poses and coordinated breathing.
ety: From Sanskrit विन्यास (vinyāsa, “disposition (of limbs)”).
examples: The occasional vinyasa class had made her more attentive to her bones. She let them give.

senses: A cask of a certain size, or its volume used as a measure of capacity. Larger than a barrel but smaller than a hogshead.
The third tone of the scale. See mediant.
A sequence of three playing cards of the same suit. Tierce of ace, king and queen is called tierce-major.
An ordinary that covers the left or right third of the field of a shield or flag.
ety: From Old French tierce, from Latin tertia.
examples: Have an eye to the molasses tierce, Mr. Stubb; it was a little leaky, I thought.

senses: To talk insincerely; to prevaricate or equivocate in speech or actions.
To give a false impression by selective use of true but misleading statements.
To babble; to chatter.
ety: Probably from Middle English *palter (“rag, trifle, worthless thing”), from Middle Low German palter (“rag, cloth”). More at paltry.
examples: Romans, that have spoke the word, And will not palter.
Who never sold the truth to serve the hour, Nor paltered with eternal God for power.
But, with a gesture, she put a period to this dalliance—one shouldn't palter so on an empty stomach, she might almost have said.

senses: A bean cake, made of fried black-eyed pea flour.
ety: Borrowed from Yoruba àkàrà. Doublet of accra.
examples: Why are you buying akara that you don't want?

senses: Large, well-built, and muscular.
ety: From Middle English burly, burely, borly, burlich, borlich, borlic (“tall, stately”), of uncertain origin. Cognate with Scots burely, burly (“rough, stout, sturdy, strong”). Perhaps from Old English *būrlīċ (“noble, stately”, literally “bowerly”), equivalent to bower + -ly; or from Old English *byrlīċ (“high, raised”), from byre (“raised area, mound”), cognate with Old High German burlīh, purlīh (“lofty, elevated, high, exalted”), related to Old High German burjan (“to raise, lift, push up”), English burgeon. However, Irish burla (“bundle, pack; burly person”) points to a different origin.
examples: He’s a big, burly rugby player who works as a landscape gardener.

senses: The instrument used for scarifying (as for example during plastering).
An implement for working and loosening the soil; often, one with teeth or shanks that does not bring up a fresh surface.
ety: From scarify + -er.
examples: You have your scarifiers to make the ground clean.

senses: An autistic person, a person with autism.
ety: From autism + -ist.
examples: Like children and animals, autists have relatively rudimentary conceptual lives.

senses: A dry-cured ham from Italy, thinly sliced.
ety: Borrowed from Italian prosciutto (meaning 'ham', in general), from asciutto, with a change of prefix, or from a Vulgar Latin *perexsūctus, from per + Latin exsūctus.
examples: In front of him, on a low table, a plate of prosciutto, olives and cheese.

Chic cosmopolitan design meets authentic pizza Napoletana in more than a dozen styles, including the red sauce capriciosa — with artichokes, Taggiasca olives and prosciutto cotto — and white-sauce speck and mascarpone.

senses: Unsuitable for some particular purpose.
Happening/occurring at an inconvenient or inappropriate time.
ety: From Latin inopportūnus. By surface analysis, in- + opportune.
examples: That was a most inopportune spot for a picnic.
The inopportune arrival of the bus cut short the interesting conversation.
The object is to keep the yard operators apprised of main-line movements, so that they do not plan to occupy the main lines with activity into or out of the yard at an inopportune juncture.

senses: Being attracted to all genders (sometimes distinguished from pansexual by saying omnisexual attraction may still take account of gender or prefer particular genders).
Androgynous, exhibiting traits of all sexes.
Having or exhibiting sexuality everywhere.
ety: From omni- + -sexual.
examples: There was something in this that made our relationship more than homosexual, and more than heterosexual. Perhaps it could be called an omnisexual relationship.
In short, all readers can share, consciously and/or unconsciously, Whitman’s omnisexual vision—omnisexual in the all-encompassing sense of embracing auto-, homo-, and heteroerotic impulses.
Psyche’s participation in the archetypical patterns of heroic action logically implies that heroism itself is an asexual or omnisexual archetype.

senses: One who roves about for prey; one who prowls.
A person who moves stealthily around a place with intention to commit a crime, especially burglary or theft.
ety: From prowl + -er.
examples: Discourage nighttime prowlers by installing motion-sensitive lights.

senses: A small, hollow case of choux pastry with a filling.
ety: Borrowed from French profiterole.
examples: Dover sole, and Oeufs Mornay Profiteroles and Peach Flambe The waiters dance on fingertips The nights we dine at Hotel Ritz

senses: Holy basil, Ocimum tenuiflorum.
ety: Borrowed from Hindi तुलसी (tulsī), from Sanskrit तुलसी (tulasī).
examples: It was a long, long time since I had been to Rohala and while I recalled some of the rooms and the courtyard with the fountain and the tulsi plant, I had no memories of the exterior of the house I was looking for.

senses: A traditional Japanese shortsword, typically 30cm to 60cm (or nearly 12 inches to approx. 23.6 inches) in length, often used as a secondary weapon to a katana.
ety: From Japanese 脇差(わきざし) (wakizashi).
examples: Hiro shoves Reason back into the zodiac, jumps in, and starts the motor. He doesn’t have time to untie the boat from the pontoon, so he snaps through the line with his wakizashi and takes off.

senses: Any of a group of minute unicellular algae having a siliceous covering of great delicacy, now categorized as class Diatomophyceae or division Bacillariophyta.
ety: From (deprecated) genus name Diatoma, from Ancient Greek διάτομος (diátomos, “cut through, cut in half”).
examples: Diatoms are enclosed in two shells that fit together like a pillbox.
Diatoms are characterized by a cell wall called a fistula made of silica, which usually has two overlapping sections.

senses: trivial, silly and irritating.
ety: From footle + -ing.
examples: He was explaining to her things about the air service. . . . "Isn't it rather dangerous work?" she asked. She felt it was a footling question even as she asked it.
Only a couple of days ago I was compelled to take him off a case because his handling of it was so footling.
For 28 footling days the 58-nation General Assembly had been debating the now-famous U.S. afterthought: to postpone partition and substitute a U.N. trusteeship for Palestine.

senses: An individual who receives an income, usually interest, rent, dividends, capital gains, or profits from his or her assets and investments.
ety: Borrowed from French rentier.
examples: If today’s capitalists are mere lazy rentiers who contribute nothing to the production process, don’t they deserve to be downgraded to the status of feudal landlords?

senses: Resembling soap.
Full of soap.
Covered in soap.
Resembling a soap opera.
Committing or involving flattery.
ety: From soap + -y. Compare German Low German sepig (“soapy”), German seifig (“soapy”), Swedish såpig (“soapy”).
examples: Bases dissolve skin oils and have a soapy feel to them.
The dishwasher uses hot soapy water to clean the dishes and silverware.
His skin was still soapy after the shower.

senses: One who sends mail.
A computer program that sends electronic mail.
A packet or container designed for postal use.
A mailshot; advertising sent by mail.
ety: From mail + -er.
examples: Large and frequent mailers may send material on a monthly basis to their house lists, test acquisitions several times a year to drum up new donors, and perhaps do a few special appeals on top of that.
The cassette came in a brown paper mailer.
Do they recall your latest mailer? Did you ever sell an armoire through ads on hard-rock radio? Find out with low-cost "intercept" surveys of customers as they leave the store.

senses: A ticket book, a collection of tickets in the form of a booklet often sold at a discount to single tickets.
An admission pass.
ety: From French carnet (“notebook”), from Middle French quernet (“group of four sheets”).
examples: Rather than buy each ticket individually, you can buy a carnet of ten tickets for a lower price.
